sources.title: ColorSource finds the soul in Signature Theatre's re-invention of A Chorus Line
sources.notes: Named designer account with venue constraints; manufacturer supplied article.

observations.observation: The designer describes a progression from clean, restrained looks toward more energetic dance looks across the show.
observations.applicability: Large theatrical pop concert with a clear set arc.
observations.limitations: The article does not provide a cue list or independent audience study.
observations.context: Theatrical staging and a 66-date arena tour.
observations.teaching_note: Treat progression as a design hypothesis: make structural energy changes legible before adding more intensity.

observations.observation: A predominantly single-profile rig was selected for visual consistency and scale rather than maximum fixture variety.
observations.applicability: Large touring productions where repeatability and uniformity matter.
observations.limitations: This is a designer preference in one production, not a universal equipment rule.
observations.context: 164 predominant profile fixtures plus a small follow-spot complement.
observations.teaching_note: Resource richness can come from disciplined consistency, not only from adding fixture families.

observations.observation: Cool-to-warm gradients and restrained gobo use were used to differentiate looks while preserving a clean visual language.
observations.applicability: Shows with a consistent scenic frame and controlled color palette.
observations.limitations: Exact colors, cue timing and saturation values are not published.
observations.context: Backdrop trusses and a central scenic figure.
observations.teaching_note: A small palette shift can create a new section without spending a signature movement effect.

observations.observation: A floor-based V arrangement was used as a framing device so the artist remained visually legible from large venues.
observations.applicability: Arena and stadium shows with a single primary performer.
observations.limitations: The source describes intent and placement but not all cue states.
observations.context: Large audiences and a central performer frame.
observations.teaching_note: Protect the subject with a dedicated focus layer before building spectacle around it.

observations.observation: Beam sparkle was introduced near the opening of the English set as an audience-excitement signature, while later songs used larger aerial movement.
observations.applicability: Artist-led arena shows where an early signature moment is intentional.
observations.limitations: The source does not define the complete effect density or duration.
observations.context: Opening-song sparkle and a later dramatic movement number.
observations.teaching_note: Early effects are not automatically wrong; reserve them only when the opening is deliberately the signature reveal.

observations.observation: Seven reusable environments were created so a large song pool could change nightly while keeping a coherent look and feel.
observations.applicability: Improvisational bands with variable set lists.
observations.limitations: The article does not expose the underlying cue data or exact environment boundaries.
observations.context: Bluegrass tour with approximately 270 possible songs and nightly set-list variation.
observations.teaching_note: Variation can be parameterized as a small set of reusable environments rather than one bespoke cue per song.

observations.observation: Individual lighting pods were used to isolate band members and highlight solos within a larger ensemble rig.
observations.applicability: Band shows where individual musicians take turns as the focus.
observations.limitations: No cue-by-cue solo timing or intensity values are available.
observations.context: V-shaped riser arrangement with dedicated lighting pods.
observations.teaching_note: A focus layer can be spatially selective even when the overall rig is large.

observations.observation: The rig was arranged to light the band and architectural roof while preserving the video surfaces, with beams reading differently when tightened or opened.
observations.applicability: Concerts where lighting must coexist with prominent scenic or video architecture.
observations.limitations: The article does not provide the full spatial plot or programming notes.
observations.context: Slat roof, angled video walls and four trusses.
observations.teaching_note: Spatial depth is a compositional constraint: preserve negative space around scenic surfaces instead of filling every output channel.

observations.observation: High-output units were chosen to reach a tall roof and create shafts through it, while still supporting band visibility.
observations.applicability: Large live rigs with high trim and multiple visual planes.
observations.limitations: The source describes equipment intent, not a complete hierarchy of cue usage.
observations.context: Approximately 50-foot trim and a slatted scenic roof.
observations.teaching_note: Reserve output and beam contrast for moments where the architecture makes them legible.

observations.observation: A compact play used color-capable LED sources to distinguish seasons, day/night and a canvas-focused dramatic moment.
observations.applicability: Narrative theatre in compact venues with a small cast and strong scenic context.
observations.limitations: The article does not publish the full color palette or cue schedule.
observations.context: Esplanade Theatre Studio; seven primary LED sources plus focused scenic accents.
observations.teaching_note: Color can carry narrative time and attention without requiring more fixtures or higher intensity.

observations.observation: A head-height side source backlit a frosted entrance so a character could read as a silhouette without adding a large overhead rig.
observations.applicability: Small narrative spaces where scenic openings and silhouettes carry meaning.
observations.limitations: The account is descriptive and not an independent measurement of audience readability.
observations.context: Compact studio theatre with a frosted window and entrance.
observations.teaching_note: A single carefully placed layer can create depth and story more efficiently than blanket coverage.

observations.observation: Fourteen side-positioned LED spots were used to solve a constrained three-sided scenic box and still support both ensemble and solo looks.
observations.applicability: Theatre designs with blocked top light and a strong side-light vocabulary.
observations.limitations: The source does not describe the full instrument inventory or cue stack.
observations.context: Seven fixtures on each side at boom height.
observations.teaching_note: Adapt the layer architecture to the available positions; do not treat a missing conventional position as a failure.

observations.observation: The same side-light system supported saturated ensemble montage looks as well as subtle corrections for solo numbers.
observations.applicability: Dance and theatre pieces that alternate ensemble scale with individual stories.
observations.limitations: No exact cue values or transition times are provided.
observations.context: A Chorus Line re-invention with eighteen lead characters.
observations.teaching_note: One layer can serve different narrative scales when intensity, color and selectivity are independently controlled.

observations.observation: Subtle color correction and moonlight tones were used for quieter solo moments instead of keeping every look saturated and flashy.
observations.applicability: Narrative productions balancing spectacle with character clarity.
observations.limitations: The source is a designer interview in a manufacturer article and lacks independent cue review.
observations.context: Color matching to costumes and skin tone was part of the design process.
observations.teaching_note: Quiet looks are an active contrast tool, not an absence of design.

observations.observation: Improvisational music was supported by reusable environments and controlled variation rather than a single fixed look for every song.
observations.applicability: A hypothesis for translating the documented environment approach into an effect-density rule.
observations.limitations: The source does not state an effect count or prescribe when effects appear.
observations.context: Derived from the seven-environment and nightly-variation description.
observations.teaching_note: Keep this as a testable interpretation, not a direct claim about the designer's cue programming.

observations.observation: The design combines a performer frame, audience-facing effects and later aerial movement as distinct layers rather than one continuous maximum state.
observations.applicability: Visual reading of the documented rig concept, not a verified cue-by-cue reconstruction.
observations.limitations: Photography and editorial selection cannot prove timing, intensity or complete fixture coverage.
observations.context: Frame, front-truss audience effects and later movement described in the source.
observations.teaching_note: Use as a design-review question: which layer is carrying the section, and which layers are being held back?

observations.observation: Beam tightness and openness were used as distinct spatial textures around the band's scenic roof.
observations.applicability: Concerts with a scenic overhead structure and multiple beam planes.
observations.limitations: The source does not state how often the texture changes or whether it is effect-driven.
observations.context: Domino fixtures were tightened for shafts and opened to light the roof.
observations.teaching_note: A movement or beam resource can have more than one job; context determines whether it reads as texture or climax.
